title: The Agency Gap: How Generative AI Literacy Shapes Independent Writing after AI Support
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether students’ generative AI (GenAI) literacy affects how well they can write independently after AI support is removed. The authors focus on what they call the “agency gap,” meaning the extent to which students’ GenAI literacy matters more when they must independently decide how to use AI support rather than being guided through it. The study asks whether GenAI literacy predicts writing performance during AI-supported work and after AI removal, whether this depends on chatbot interaction style, and whether the relationship persists after accounting for domain-specific visualisation literacy.

The intervention compared two AI support conditions for multimodal academic writing: a reactive chatbot that only answered student-initiated questions, and a proactive chatbot that actively scaffolded students through structured prompts and feedback. Participants first completed an AI-supported writing task using one of these chatbot types, then completed a parallel writing task without AI support. Writing was assessed with an objective rubric across insightfulness, visual data integration, organisation and coherence, linguistic quality, and critical thinking. The study also measured GenAI literacy using the GLAT and visualisation literacy using the mini-VLAT.

The population was 79 participants recruited via Prolific who were current students or graduates from medical or nursing programs. The context was higher education and involved online multimodal academic writing tasks based on healthcare simulation visualisations. Participants were randomly assigned to either the reactive or proactive chatbot condition. Although the participants came from multiple world regions, the paper does not report a single study country for the sample; the institutional affiliations are in Australia and China.

The main conclusion is that GenAI literacy predicted stronger independent writing performance only in the reactive chatbot condition, especially after AI support was removed. In the proactive condition, proactive scaffolding appeared to reduce differences between students with lower and higher GenAI literacy. Mediation analyses showed that the effect was not explained by better AI-supported performance transferring forward; instead, GenAI literacy functioned as a more direct, task-general competence. The authors argue that educators should both build students’ GenAI literacy and design proactive AI scaffolds to reduce inequities when learners cannot be assumed to use AI strategically on their own.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family conversational generative AI system used here as the underlying multimodal LLM for chatbot-based support.
identified_tools.use_case: The study implemented two custom academic-writing support chatbots (reactive and proactive) powered by the multimodal GPT-4o model to assist students with multimodal academic writing based on visual data, followed by a parallel writing task without AI support.

findings.finding_summary: In the reactive chatbot condition, GenAI literacy was positively associated with independent writing performance after AI removal across insightfulness (rs=.41, p=.010), visual data integration (rs=.40, p=.013), organisation and coherence (rs=.44, p=.005), linguistic quality (rs=.32, p=.045), critical thinking (rs=.37, p=.019), and composite score (rs=.44, p=.005). No significant correlations were observed in the proactive condition, indicating that proactive scaffolding equalised outcomes across GenAI literacy levels.
findings.measure: Academic writing rubric scores after AI removal: insightfulness, visual data integration, organisation and coherence, linguistic quality, critical thinking, composite score

findings.finding_summary: Mann-Whitney tests showed that in the reactive condition, high-GenAI-literacy students outperformed low-literacy students at AI-removal on insightfulness (U=99.00, p=.021, rrb=.34), visual data integration (U=87.50, p=.012, rrb=.36), organisation and coherence (U=67.50, p=.002, rrb=.46), and composite score (U=83.50, p=.009, rrb=.41). In the proactive condition, no significant differences between low- and high-GenAI-literacy groups were found on any rubric metric at either time point.
findings.measure: Group differences in rubric scores by GenAI literacy level at AI-support and AI-removal stages
findings.effect_size: rrb=.28 to .46 for significant reactive-condition contrasts

findings.finding_summary: Ordinal logistic regression showed that higher GenAI literacy significantly predicted stronger post-AI-removal writing performance for visual data integration (b=0.13, SE=0.06, z=2.07, p=.039, OR=1.14), critical thinking (b=0.14, SE=0.07, z=2.18, p=.029, OR=1.15), and composite writing score (b=0.10, SE=0.05, z=2.15, p=.032, OR=1.11), controlling for domain knowledge, chatbot type, and AI-supported performance. Domain knowledge and chatbot type were not significant predictors in these models.
findings.measure: Ordinal logistic regression predicting AI-removal writing scores

findings.finding_summary: Bootstrap mediation analyses found no significant indirect effect of GenAI literacy on independent writing performance through AI-supported writing performance in either condition. In the reactive condition, the indirect effect was 0.032 with 95% CI [-0.022, 0.108]; in the proactive condition, the indirect effect was 0.022 with 95% CI [-0.055, 0.102].
findings.measure: Indirect effect of GenAI literacy on AI-removal writing via AI-support performance

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical experimental study with random assignment to reactive versus proactive chatbot conditions, but the main reported effects are correlational/associational with a relatively small sample (n=79), rather than a clean causal estimate of the tool's impact on achievement versus a non-AI control. Accordingly, it fits a yellow tier under the framework provided.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported associations and group differences are modest to moderate in size, especially in the reactive condition (e.g., rs up to .44, rank-biserial correlations up to .46, OR up to 1.15). Effects are not uniformly present across conditions, so impact is better characterized as modest rather than consistently large.
